```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.8,
                      fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
```

This vignette reproduces the main map of the application in the package's paper:
cockroach hot and cold spots in Madrid, summers 2010--2012, on a 1 km grid,
after adjusting for exposure and environmental covariates (model M2).

```{r}
library(hotcoldESF)
dim(madrid)
```

`madrid` has one row per cell, with the reports per year and the covariates;
`madrid_A` is the queen contiguity matrix of the cells, and `madrid_boundary` the
outline of the city (see `?madrid`).

## Reports and covariates

We pool the cockroach reports of the summers (April--September) of 2010, 2011 and
2012, and keep 2013 to check the priority list later.

```{r data}
Y <- with(madrid, cockroaches_2010 + cockroaches_2011 + cockroaches_2012)
sum(Y)
```

Reports depend on how many people live in a cell and can see a pest. The model
therefore includes exposure (number of residential address points, population
density, cell area) and the environmental risk factors (green areas, age of the
buildings, water, drinking fountains, cat-feeding points, unemployment).

```{r covariates}
Z <- with(madrid, cbind(log_residential = log1p(residential), density,
                        log_area = log(area), dist_green, green_area, year_built,
                        dist_water, dist_fountain, dist_cat, unemployment))
summary(lm(log1p(Y) ~ Z))$r.squared
```

The covariates explain most of the variation of the log counts. The question is
where the rest is concentrated.

## Hot and cold spots

```{r fit}
set.seed(2026)
h <- hot_cold_map(Y, Z, madrid_A)
h
```

A helper draws the cells as 1 km squares inside the city outline.

```{r helper}
draw <- function(col, main) {
  plot(NA, xlim = range(madrid$x) + c(-500, 500), ylim = range(madrid$y) + c(-500, 500),
       asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main, font.main = 1, cex.main = 0.9)
  rect(madrid$x - 500, madrid$y - 500, madrid$x + 500, madrid$y + 500, col = col, border = "white", lwd = 0.3)
  for (r in unique(madrid_boundary$ring))
    with(madrid_boundary[madrid_boundary$ring == r, ], polygon(x, y, border = "grey30"))
}
greens <- colorRampPalette(c("#f2f7ee", "#a8d08d", "#4d9a3a", "#1f5f1a"))(100)
```

```{r maps, fig.height = 3.8}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
draw(greens[cut(log1p(Y), 100, labels = FALSE)], "log(1 + reports), summers 2010-2012")
draw(c(hot = "#e34948", neutral = "#f0efec", cold = "#2a78d6")[as.character(h$labels)],
     "hot (red) and cold (blue) cells, model M2")
par(op)
```

The cells with most reports follow where people live. Once exposure and the
environment are accounted for, the hot cells form a band across the south-centre
of the city and an area in the north-centre.

```{r summary}
c(hot = sum(h$labels == "hot"), cold = sum(h$labels == "cold"),
  share_of_reports_in_hot_cells = round(sum(Y[h$labels == "hot"]) / sum(Y), 2))
```

## Priority list and the following summer

If a control campaign can only cover 25 cells, `rank_cells()` gives them: hot cells
first, ordered by their estimated excess. We check how many of the 2013 reports fall
in those cells, against the 25 cells with most reports in 2010--2012.

```{r rank}
top_esf    <- rank_cells(h)[1:25]
top_counts <- order(-Y)[1:25]
c(esf = sum(madrid$cockroaches_2013[top_esf]),
  counts = sum(madrid$cockroaches_2013[top_counts])) / sum(madrid$cockroaches_2013)
```

Ranking by counts captures more of next year's reports, because reports follow
exposure, which does not change from one year to the next. The covariate-adjusted
list targets a different question: where there are more reports than the
characteristics of the area explain. The paper discusses this trade-off and suggests
using the hot zones to decide where to act and the counts or residuals to order the
cells within them.
